A0155.title: Decentralized On-Chain Identity Verification
A0155.definition: The use of decentralized identity technologies such as DID to achieve identity verification without relying on centralized authorities.
A0155.description: DID scheme: W3C DID standard; on-chain identity anchor; verifiable credentials; selective disclosure; self-sovereign identity; cross-platform mutual recognition.
A0155.limitation: Once the private keys of DID documents and verifiable credentials are phished or stolen by endpoint malware, an attacker can impersonate the identity using legitimate credentials, and the verification mechanism cannot distinguish the true operator from the impostor; resolution and trust anchor implementations across DID methods (did:web, did:ethr, etc.) are not unified, and differences in verifier implementations may cause false positives or false negatives; selective disclosure under zero-knowledge proof implementations incurs high computational overhead, making mobile deployment difficult; the ecosystem is immature and regulatory acceptance is low, and delays in revocation registry updates can cause revoked credentials to be mistakenly treated as valid within the window period.

references.title: Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0 - W3C

A0155-001.title: Decentralized Identity Credential Verification
A0155-001.description: Perform on-chain/off-chain joint verification of DID resolution, verifiable credential (VC) issuer signatures, revocation status, expiration time, and presentation policies to confirm that the credential has not been forged or revoked before granting business access. Cover the full lifecycle of credential issuance, holding, presentation, and verification to prevent attackers from forging identity credentials to impersonate others or gain unauthorized access.
A0155-001.definition: Verify DID and VC issuers, revocation status, and presentation policies to reduce credential forgery risk.
A0155-001.limitation: If the private keys of DID documents and VCs are phished or stolen by endpoint malware, an attacker can impersonate a legitimate holder, and the verification mechanism cannot distinguish the real operator. Revocation registry update delays may cause revoked credentials to be incorrectly treated as valid within the lag window. Selective disclosure under zero-knowledge proof implementations incurs high computational overhead, making mobile deployment difficult. Cross-DID method resolution (e.g., did:web, did:ethr) varies significantly; inconsistent verifier implementations may lead to false positives or false negatives.
